Where it began

Sourav Ganguly was born in Calcutta on 8 July 1972, in a city that loved football first. Cricket ran in the family, though. His older brother Snehasish had made his name in the Bengal side, and he made sure Sourav got a place at a coaching camp one summer holiday.

Sourav was right-handed, yet he learned to bat left-handed so that he could use his brother's kit. It turned out to be a very good idea. The brothers practised on a concrete pitch at home and studied old videos of David Gower, the batsman Sourav most admired.

The player

After a single one-day game in 1992, he went back to domestic cricket and piled up runs, and an innings of 171 in the Duleep Trophy earned him a place on the 1996 tour of England. On his Test debut at Lord's, in the same match as Rahul Dravid, he made 131, which set a new record for a debutant at the ground.

He played 113 Tests and made 7,212 runs at 42.18, with 16 hundreds and a best of 239 against Pakistan in December 2007, his first double hundred. His medium pace brought him 32 wickets as well. In one-day cricket he and Sachin Tendulkar formed a great opening pair, and at the 1999 World Cup he made 183 against Sri Lanka at Taunton.

What made him special

On the off side he had few equals: Dravid once ranked him just behind God in that part of the field. Above all, he was a leader. Made captain in 2000, he led India in 49 Tests and won 21, at the time more than any Indian captain. His side ended Australia's run of 16 Test wins in a row in 2001, took the 2002 Champions Trophy and reached the 2003 World Cup final. He backed young players and gave them time to settle.

Running between the wickets was not his strongest suit, and more than one partner learned to watch his calls carefully.

Away from the middle

He was awarded the Padma Shri in 2004. After leaving Test cricket he hosted Dadagiri Unlimited, a Bengali television quiz with contestants from all over West Bengal, and in 2018 he published his autobiography, A Century Is Not Enough. He ran the Cricket Association of Bengal from 2015 to 2019 and in 2019 was elected to lead Indian cricket's governing board as its president. His wife, Dona Ganguly, is a classical dancer of note in her own right.

And finally

His Test career had a neat symmetry. He began it with a hundred on debut and finished it with a first-ball dismissal in his final innings, the only batsman to manage that particular pair of bookends.
